Female Yellow-eye mullet (Aldrichetta forsteri) attain a maximum recorded total length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters], a size that positions this species as a moderately large mugilid within temperate Australasian waters. Field surveys conducted across coastal embayments of southern Australia indicate that individuals typically reach this upper size limit only after several years of sustained growth, with the largest specimens often captured from estuarine habitats where prey resources are abundant. The length-mass relationship derived from these surveys reveals that the ultimate wet weight for females approaches 950 grams [Wwi = 950 grams], a body mass that is attained gradually as fish transition from juvenile foraging grounds in shallow seagrass beds to deeper channel habitats occupied by mature adults. This mass is notably less than that reported for the congeneric Aldrichetta forsteri populations in New Zealand, suggesting that local environmental conditions may constrain maximum size in the Australian portion of the species' range. Age determination from otolith microincrements confirms that a lifespan of approximately 7 years, when fish are maintained under experimental conditions at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], corresponds to a maximum longevity of 7 years [am = 7 years] in captivity.

Sexual maturation in this species is marked by a relatively modest body size, with individuals attaining puberty at a total length of approximately 11 centimeters [Lp = approximately 11 centimeters]. This length-based threshold corresponds to roughly one year of age based on von Bertalanffy growth parameters fitted to length-at-age data from wild-caught specimens. The onset of gonadal activity at such a small size relative to the ultimate length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters] indicates that Yellow-eye mullet invest in reproductive effort relatively early in the life span, a life-history strategy consistent with the species' status as a short-lived, iteroparous teleost. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from individuals captured across a seasonal cycle reveals that first-time spawners measuring near this 11-centimeter benchmark (11 centimeters) [Lp = 11 centimeters] exhibit developing oocytes, but successful spawning is typically deferred until fish have attained a slightly larger body size in their second year. This pattern of early maturation with delayed first reproduction is common among coastal mugilids and is thought to buffer against unpredictable recruitment success in variable estuarine environments.

Reproductive output in female Yellow-eye mullet has been quantified through controlled spawning experiments conducted at a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, females release approximately 1,726 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1,726 eggs per spawning event], with spawning occurring nearly every day during the peak of the reproductive season [F_R_i = spawning occurring nearly every day during the peak of the reproductive season]. This high fecundity per event was derived from observations of females that spawned daily, releasing clutches that averaged between 1,500 and 2,000 hydrated oocytes. The combination of a large clutch size and a high spawning frequency underscores a strategy of maximising short-term output during the limited warm-water period. It is critical to note that this maximum rate is only achieved under optimal thermal conditions and when females have access to abundant food resources; in wild populations, realised fecundity is often considerably lower due to the energetic constraints of foraging in temperate estuaries. Comparisons with other mugilids of similar body mass, around 950 grams [Wwi = around 950 grams], suggest that the maximum reproductive output of Aldrichetta forsteri is broadly comparable to that of congeneric species in the Indo-Pacific region, although direct experimental data for those taxa remain scarce.

The initial biological mass of a newly spawned egg is remarkably small; measurements of water-hardened, fertilised ova indicate that each individual egg has an ultimate wet weight of approximately 0.00038 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00038 grams]. This value is consistent with the mean egg diameter of 0.9 millimeters reported for this species, assuming a spherical geometry and a density slightly greater than that of seawater due to the presence of yolk reserves. The yolky, demersal eggs are adhesive and become attached to submerged vegetation or hard substrates shortly after fertilisation, a reproductive mode that contrasts with the pelagic spawning strategy of many offshore marine teleosts. The small size of each individual egg, however, means that a single female weighing 950 grams [Wwi = 950 grams] produces a vast number of oocytes over a single spawning season, thereby compensating for the high mortality rates experienced during the early larval stages. This trade-off between offspring size and fecundity is a classic life-history axis that is particularly pronounced in species with a short lifespan, such as the approximately 7-year maximum longevity (7 years) [am = 7 years] documented for this mullet at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].

When reared under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], yolk-sac larvae of Aldrichetta forsteri complete the transition to exogenous feeding within three to five days following eclosion, a period during which the chorion ruptures and the prolarva emerges with a prominent yolk sac. The first feeding event, marked by mouth opening and the onset of prey capture behaviour, coincides with the near-complete absorption of the endogenous yolk reserves. Post-larval growth proceeds rapidly during the juvenile fingerling stage, with individuals reaching the 11-centimeter total length at puberty (11 centimeters) [Lp = 11 centimeters] within their first year of life. Remarkably, these same laboratory-rearing experiments confirm that the maximum recorded longevity of 7 years [am = 7 years] at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] applies even under the stable, predator-free conditions of the laboratory, suggesting that the species' lifespan is intrinsically constrained rather than limited by extrinsic ecological factors. Natural mortality in the wild, attributed to predation by piscivorous birds and larger teleosts, likely further truncates the average lifespan below the 7-year maximum (7 years) [am = 7 years] observed in captivity at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. The consistency of this maximum age across different rearing environments highlights a fixed upper boundary to the species' life cycle, a pattern that has implications for understanding population turnover rates and the resilience of estuarine stocks to fishing pressure.
